text: Your company runs a niche internal inventory system with no official ServiceNow spoke — a homegrown platform reachable only over its own REST API. Multiple teams keep asking the same question inside their flows: does this item still have stock? Right now, every flow builder either drops in a generic REST step and configures the inventory API by hand, or asks a developer to write a Script step. Neither scales. Your task: design a reusable custom action, Check Inventory Level, so any flow builder can ask that question without touching the inventory system's API.

Step one is defining the Input. The inventory API identifies items by SKU, so the action needs exactly one required Input: Item SKU, a string. You don't add inputs for warehouse location or an API key — those belong to the internal step and the Authentication Profile, not the flow builder. Step two is the internal REST step: a GET call to the real endpoint, SKU substituted in, authenticating through a Chapter 3 Authentication Profile referenced here rather than re-entered.

The inventory system returns a JSON body with sku, qty_available, and warehouse. Step three is defining the Outputs, and you don't expose every field the API returned — only what a consumer needs. That's a single Output, Quantity Available, mapped from qty_available. You leave out warehouse and the raw SKU echo; they're internal details of the lookup, not something a flow deciding whether an order can be fulfilled needs to see.

Step four is the sanity check Lesson 18 described. The Input name, Item SKU, is clear to anyone who's never seen the inventory system. The single Output, Quantity Available, is exactly what a consumer flow needs and nothing more. The Authentication Profile is the inventory team's shared service account, not a personal credential that breaks when someone leaves.

With that check passed, the action is ready to publish. Any flow builder in the company can now drop Check Inventory Level into a flow, supply a SKU, and read back a quantity, with no idea the inventory system's REST API even exists underneath — the custom action pattern from Lesson 18, worked through end to end.

That closes Chapter 5 on IntegrationHub — what it adds, how Spokes and Connector Actions are structured, how to build a custom action, and now how to design one against a real scenario. Next up: Chapter 6 opens with designing for integration failures, what happens when a call to an external system doesn't go the way you expected.
